guidance: Ask whether spoken, written, visual, AAC, or extra processing time helps.
Treat communication difference as a support need, not defiance.
Reduce sound, light, touch, crowding, and competing demands when possible.
Offer exit, headphones, dimmer space, or fewer simultaneous instructions.
Give concrete notice before changes.
Explain what is changing, what stays the same, and what happens next.
Prioritize safety and reduce demands.
Use fewer words and avoid arguing, teaching, or punishment during peak overload.
Allow reduced speech and lower-demand communication.
Support basic needs and recovery time without forcing immediate explanation.
Allow safe self-regulatory movement or repetition.
Redirect only when the behavior is unsafe, harmful, or the person asks for alternatives.
Do not make appearing non-autistic the primary goal.
Support authentic communication, sensory needs, and recovery from sustained social effort.
Break multistep tasks into visible concrete actions.
Use routines, checklists, visual schedules, or environmental cues when preferred.
Use concrete body check-ins for hunger, thirst, pain, temperature, toileting, and fatigue.
Do not assume delayed body awareness means symptoms are unimportant.
Document communication and sensory accommodations before visits.
List known triggers, preferred support person roles, and consent preferences.
A chat can organize traits and questions but cannot establish an autism diagnosis.
Encourage qualified evaluation when formal diagnosis or documentation is needed.
